tagline.text: A sunset beach south of El Nido town, also known as Las Cabañas

children.text: A golden-sand beach about 5 km south of El Nido town, 10–15 minutes by tricycle. There is no entrance fee, and the bars and restaurants along it make it one of the best places in El Nido to watch the sunset.
Marimegmeg is El Nido's sunset beach, sometimes written "Marimjam" in Korean sources. It lies about
5 km

south of the center of El Nido town, along the road past Corong-Corong beach. It runs into Las Cabañas Beach and Vanilla Beach and is effectively one long beach, and the names are mixed up even on maps, so when asking directions, use both "Las Cabañas" and "Marimegmeg." It was once a fishing village with no notable monuments, and despite the resort development it is described as keeping a fairly quiet, sustainability-minded atmosphere.

The appeal here is the hour around sunset. The sand is closer to golden than the white sand you meet on island tours, and it glows softly just before sunset and at blue hour. Limestone rocks and small islands overlap across the water, and many travelers gather from about 5 p.m. to drink a beer at the beach bars and wait for the sunset. Sunset falls at about 5:30 p.m. in November and about 6:25 p.m. in June, nearly an hour of difference across the seasons.

El Nido's signature activity is island hopping, and Marimegmeg is where many people come to relax in the afternoon afterward. There is no entrance fee and you can simply stand on the beach and watch the sunset, so it suits travelers on a tight budget. There is also the Las Cabañas Zipline, which runs from the hillside above the beach across the water to Depeldet Island, so you can watch riders pass over the beach. Yoga sessions are said to be held on the beach, and a local guide recommends climbing the nearby hill before sunset for a view over Bacuit Bay along a hidden trail. You need to ask locals where it is, so do not push it and go while it is still light.

Keep your expectations modest for swimming. There is nowhere at the edge of the beach to rinse off, and a permanent roadside sign is said to warn of jellyfish. Check the water before going in, and stay out if anything seems off. Think of it as a place to stroll, have a drink and take photos, and you will be satisfied. Some guide sites list hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., but treat that as a rough guide, since the beach is open and people gather around sunset, and confirm on site. It is much quieter early in the morning, and the water is described as shallow with a gentle slope.
Most travelers in El Nido come here to see the sunset. It is best to arrive around 5 p.m. and find a spot, and the sunset time changes with the season.
The sand here is closer to golden than white, and it glows softly just before sunset and during the blue hour. The silhouettes of the limestone rocks make for good photos.
Bars and restaurants line the beach, and many put bean bags on the sand. Order a drink around sunset and settle in.
A zipline runs from the hillside above the beach across the water to Depeldet Island. Check the price on site; it is also fun to watch from the beach even if you do not ride.

The wide sand is popular for beach volleyball and Frisbee. Bring a ball for an easy afternoon of play. Some sources say marine life can be seen while snorkeling near parts of the beach, but check equipment and conditions on site.
Some businesses rent kayaks and stand-up paddleboards. Check availability and prices on site.

There may be no tricycles for the return, so ask your driver to wait or ask your accommodation or the bar to call one.

On a day when you have been island hopping, it is easier on your energy to come only for the afternoon sunset.

El Nido's dry season runs from December to May, when the sea is calm and the sky is clear, which is best for sunsets. Sunset times vary from about 17:30 in November to about 18:25 in June.
In the rainy season it can be cloudy with higher waves, and jellyfish are another variable, so check conditions on site.
The surf season at Lio and Duli beaches is said to run from roughly November to March. Some days can be windy then, so check sea conditions.

Directly on the beach there are resorts, hostels and guesthouses, and El Nido town offers a wider choice of lodging. Staying on the beach lets you see the sunset up close but is far from town, which can be inconvenient when moving around at night.

Cafes and bars along the beach serve everything from seafood dishes to cocktails. Many do not accept credit cards, so bring plenty of cash. There are no ATMs on the beach, and the ATMs in town sometimes have long lines or run out of cash.
The El Nido Eco-Tourism Development Fee (ETDF) for visitors arriving from outside Palawan is
for ages 14 and over and
for ages 6–13 (Palawan residents pay ₱200 and ₱150), raised from

in June 2024, and valid for 5 days (some sources say 10, so check your receipt). It is usually collected by the operator when you book island hopping, and there is also a notice that visitors arriving overland must pay at an office in Bagong Bayan, so check the latest announcements. The Big Lagoon (Tour A) and Small Lagoon (Tour D) cost an extra
, and the Matinloc Shrine has an optional
entrance fee. Marimegmeg Beach itself is free.
